French dynamiqueder. English dynamic From French dynamique, from Ancient Greek δυναμικός (dunamikós, “powerful”), from δύναμις (dúnamis, “power”), from δύναμαι (dúnamai, “I am able”).

senses.d: Changing; active; in motion.
ex: The environment is dynamic, changing with the years and the seasons.

senses.d: Powerful; energetic.
ex: He was a dynamic and engaging speaker.

senses.d: Able to change and adapt.
Having to do with the volume of sound.
ex: The dynamic marking in bar 40 is forte.

senses.d: Happening at runtime instead of being predetermined at compile time.
Pertaining to dynamics, the branch of mechanics concerned with the effects of forces on the motion of objects.
Of a verb: not stative, but fientive; indicating continued or progressive action on the part of the subject.
A characteristic or manner of an interaction; a behavior.
ex: Watch the dynamic between the husband and wife when they disagree.
One of the under-reported dynamics during the coronavirus pandemic has been the collapse of One Nation’s vote.

senses.d: A moving force.
ex: The study of fluid dynamics quantifies turbulent and laminar flows.

senses.d: The varying loudness or volume of a song or the markings that indicate the loudness.
ex: If you pay attention to the dynamics as you play, it's a very moving piece.

senses.d: A symbol in a musical score that indicates the desired level of volume.
A verb that indicates continued or progressive action on the part of the subject.

grp.label: computing: happening at runtime instead of at compile time

senses.d: The branch of mechanics that is concerned with the effects of forces on the motion of objects.
The changing amplitude or level of a sound wave or selection of audio.
The volume with which music is to be performed, denoted by such terms as piano, mezzo piano, mezzo forte, or forte.
Forces that stimulate growth, change, or development.
ex: The changing dynamics in international politics led to such an outcome.

ety.text: Borrowed from Middle French dynastie, from Late Latin dynastia, from Ancient Greek δυναστεία (dunasteía, “power, dominion”).

senses.d: A series of rulers or dynasts from one family.
ex: A dynasty is nothing but the successful orchestration of treachery.

senses.d: A family considered over time, with its ancestors and descendants
The polity or historical era under the rule of a certain dynasty.
ex: During the Ming dynasty, China was ruled by the Zhu family.

senses.d: A team or organization which has an extended period of success or dominant performance.

grp.label: a series of rulers or dynasts from one family
era or polity under a certain dynasty, especially in East Asian history

Coined by Alfred Nobel in 1867. Ultimately from Ancient Greek δύναμις (dúnamis, “power”) + -ite, most likely under the influence of dynamo or dynamic.

senses.d: A class of explosives made from nitroglycerine in an absorbent medium such as kieselguhr, used in mining and blasting.
A stick of trinitrotoluene (TNT).
Anything exceptionally dangerous, exciting or wonderful.
ex: And your shoulders are frozen (Cold as the night) / Oh, but you're an explosion (You're dynamite)

senses.d: A strong drug, in particular heroin, cocaine or potent marijuana.
To blow up with dynamite or other high explosive.
ex: Gradually the construction gangs cut and dynamited their way through some of the most difficult country in the world.

senses.d: To dismantle or destroy.
To apply maximum pressure to very quickly.
ex: Juan dynamited the brakes and the car skidded to a halt.

senses.d: To lock up from being invoked too suddenly.
